questions.stem: What separates security monitoring from a one-time security audit?

options.text: Monitoring continuously collects and analyzes logs, events, and network activity, which feeds detection and response

options.rationale: Once a year describes an audit, not monitoring.

options.text: Monitoring covers only physical security cameras
options.rationale: It covers logs, events, and network activity.
One is continuous; the other is a point-in-time check.

questions.explanation: Security monitoring is the continuous collection and analysis of logs, events, and network activity to detect threats. It is ongoing, not one-time, and it feeds detection and response.
questions.discriminator_tested: Security monitoring is ongoing, not one-time.

questions.stem: What does a SIEM add beyond simply storing logs in one place?

options.text: Correlation across many sources, which turns scattered events into meaningful alerts, plus retention

options.rationale: That is an IPS or firewall.
A SIEM analyzes events; it doesn't filter traffic.

questions.explanation: A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) collects logs from many sources, correlates events, raises alerts, and retains data. Central collection plus correlation turns scattered events into meaningful alerts.
questions.discriminator_tested: Collection plus correlation turns scattered events into alerts.

questions.stem: What is a decision about the SIEM hosting model about?

options.text: Where the SIEM runs, on-premises or in the cloud, with trade-offs in control, cost, and maintenance
Which detection algorithm the SIEM uses
options.rationale: That is the choice of detection methods.

options.text: Which regulations apply to the company
options.rationale: Regulations depend on the business, not on where the SIEM runs.

questions.explanation: The SIEM hosting model is where the SIEM runs: on-premises or in the cloud. It is a deployment choice with trade-offs in control, cost, and maintenance.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hosting model = on-premises or cloud, with control, cost, and maintenance trade-offs.

questions.stem: A defense contractor needs full control over its security data, wants that data to stay on its own premises, and has staff to maintain servers. Which kind of SIEM fits?

options.rationale: Correct: full control, and the data stays local.
A cloud SIEM is vendor-hosted, so the data leaves the premises.

options.text: No SIEM; firewall logs are enough

options.rationale: SOAR acts on detections; it doesn't replace the SIEM.

questions.explanation: With an on-prem SIEM, the organization hosts and maintains the platform. It gets full control and keeps data local, at the cost of higher upfront spending, maintenance, and scaling effort.
questions.discriminator_tested: On-prem: full control, data stays local; higher cost and maintenance.

questions.stem: A fast-growing startup with a tiny IT team wants a SIEM that scales on demand with little maintenance. Which choice fits, and what must it still consider?

options.text: A cloud SIEM; it still depends on connectivity, and where the data is stored may be a concern
options.rationale: Correct: elastic and low-maintenance, with those caveats.

options.text: An on-prem SIEM, because it needs the least maintenance
options.rationale: An on-prem SIEM needs the most maintenance.

options.text: A cloud SIEM, which needs no internet connection
options.rationale: A cloud SIEM depends on connectivity.

options.text: A cloud SIEM, which requires buying servers up front
options.rationale: Avoiding that purchase is one of its benefits.

questions.explanation: A cloud SIEM is a vendor-hosted service with elastic scaling and less maintenance. It depends on connectivity, and data location may be a concern.
questions.discriminator_tested: Cloud SIEM: elastic and low-maintenance; depends on connectivity; data location may matter.

questions.stem: Why does a SIEM combine several detection methods?

options.text: No single detection method catches everything
options.rationale: Correct: each method has blind spots.

options.text: One method is always enough; combining them is just marketing
options.rationale: Each method misses things the others catch.

questions.explanation: SIEM detection methods are the techniques a SIEM uses to spot suspicious activity. Several are combined, because no single method catches everything.
questions.discriminator_tested: Combine methods; no single method catches everything.

questions.stem: In its first week, a new SIEM floods analysts with meaningless 'unusual activity' alerts. What prerequisite is most likely missing?

options.text: A baseline of normal activity, which has to exist before deviations mean anything
options.rationale: Correct: without it, everything looks unusual.
Automating responses to bad alerts makes things worse.

questions.explanation: Baseline analysis establishes what normal activity looks like and compares current activity with it. The baseline is the reference, and it must exist before deviations mean anything.
questions.discriminator_tested: The baseline must exist before deviations mean anything.

questions.stem: An attacker uses a brand-new tool with no known signature. At 3 a.m., a file server suddenly sends 50 GB to an unfamiliar host, far outside its normal pattern. Which method flags this, and what is that method's drawback?

options.text: Anomaly detection; it can catch unknown threats but raises more false positives
Signature-based detection; it never misses anything
options.rationale: With no known signature, signature matching would miss this.

options.text: IoC matching; it needs no data at all
options.rationale: There is no known indicator for a brand-new tool.

options.text: Data locality; it flags transfers abroad
options.rationale: Data locality is a compliance requirement, not a detection method.

questions.explanation: Anomaly detection flags activity that deviates from the baseline or expected pattern. It can catch unknown threats but raises more false positives than signature-based detection.
questions.discriminator_tested: Anomaly detection catches unknown threats but raises more false positives.

questions.stem: How does machine learning in a SIEM differ from fixed correlation rules?

options.text: It learns patterns from data and reduces manual rule tuning, but it depends on good data and can still misclassify
It is identical to fixed rules
options.rationale: It learns rather than following fixed rules.

questions.explanation: Machine learning algorithms learn patterns from data to detect threats and reduce manual rule tuning. They depend on good data and can still misclassify.
questions.discriminator_tested: Machine learning learns from data; it depends on good data and can misclassify.

questions.stem: What is the right role for AI integration in a security operations center?

options.text: Helping analysts with triage, correlation, summarization, and prioritization, with results validated by humans

options.rationale: Its results still need human validation.
Unchecked AI decisions can be wrong.

questions.explanation: AI integration assists with triage, correlation, summarization, and prioritization. It augments analysts, and its results need human validation.
questions.discriminator_tested: AI augments analysts; its results need human validation.

questions.stem: A finance employee's account normally signs in from one city during business hours. It starts downloading HR files at 2 a.m. from another country. Which SIEM capability focuses on this kind of account behavior?

options.rationale: Correct: it baselines users and entities and flags unusual behavior.
That is external context about known bad indicators.
SOAR responds; it doesn't model user behavior.

questions.explanation: UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) baselines users and devices and flags unusual behavior. It focuses on how accounts and entities behave, which helps find compromised accounts and insider threats.
questions.discriminator_tested: UEBA focuses on the behavior of accounts and entities.

questions.stem: What separates threat intelligence data from a baseline?

options.text: Threat intelligence is external context (known malicious IPs, domains, hashes, and techniques); a baseline describes your own normal activity

options.rationale: One comes from outside; the other is built internally.

options.text: A baseline comes from external feeds
options.rationale: A baseline is built from your own activity.

options.text: Threat intelligence describes only your internal behavior

questions.explanation: Threat intelligence data comes from external feeds of known malicious IPs, domains, hashes, and attacker techniques. It provides external context, in contrast to an internal baseline.
questions.discriminator_tested: Threat intelligence is external; the baseline is internal.

questions.stem: Which two of these are IoCs (indicators of compromise)? (Choose two.)

options.text: A file whose hash matches known ransomware
Outbound connections to a domain listed as a known command-and-control server

questions.explanation: An IoC (indicator of compromise) is observable evidence that a system may be compromised, such as malicious IPs, file hashes, domains, or unusual changes. IoCs are often delivered through threat intelligence.
questions.discriminator_tested: An IoC is evidence of compromise.

questions.stem: How is the work divided between a SIEM and SOAR?

options.text: The SIEM detects and correlates; SOAR acts on what was detected, using playbooks

options.rationale: One detects and the other responds.
Storing and correlating logs is the SIEM's job.

questions.explanation: SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) coordinates tools and automates response workflows (playbooks). The SIEM detects and correlates; SOAR acts on what was detected.
questions.discriminator_tested: The SIEM detects; SOAR acts.

questions.stem: A playbook takes a phishing alert, queries threat intelligence, searches every mailbox, quarantines the matching emails, blocks the sender at the email gateway, and opens a ticket. Is this orchestration or automation?

options.text: Orchestration: it coordinates many tools and steps into one workflow, and individual steps may themselves be automated
Automation only, because it is a single task
options.rationale: It spans several tools and tasks.
The playbook runs the steps itself.

questions.explanation: Orchestration vs automation: orchestration coordinates multiple tools and tasks into a workflow; automation performs a single task without human action.
questions.discriminator_tested: Orchestration = many steps and tools; automation = one task.

questions.stem: What separates regulations and compliance obligations from internal policy?

options.text: They are external legal and industry requirements, and failing them risks fines and legal action
They are set internally by each company
They are the same as internal policy
options.rationale: One is externally imposed; the other is internal.

questions.explanation: Regulations and compliance are legal and industry requirements for protecting data; failure risks fines and legal action. They are external obligations, unlike internal policy.
questions.discriminator_tested: Regulations are external obligations with penalties.

questions.stem: A European company considers a cloud SIEM hosted only in the United States. Its legal team objects, because customer log data must stay within the EU. Which requirement is this?

options.rationale: Correct: it concerns where the data physically resides.
That protects card data and doesn't set storage regions.
That applies to US federal agencies.

questions.explanation: Data locality is a requirement that data be stored or processed in specific geographic jurisdictions. It is about where data physically resides, and it affects cloud choices.
questions.discriminator_tested: Data locality = where data physically resides.

questions.stem: A US university must protect its students' grades and transcripts. Which law applies?

options.rationale: PCI DSS covers payment card data.

questions.explanation: FERPA (Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act) protects student education records in the US.
questions.discriminator_tested: FERPA = education records.

questions.stem: A US federal agency must run an information security program for its systems. Which law requires this?
questions.explanation: FISMA (Federal Information Security Modernization Act) requires US federal agencies to run information security programs. It covers federal government systems.
questions.discriminator_tested: FISMA = federal government systems.

questions.stem: A US bank must protect its customers' nonpublic personal financial information. Which law applies?

options.rationale: That governs where data is stored, not the bank's duty to protect it.

questions.explanation: GLBA (Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act) requires financial institutions to protect customers' nonpublic personal information.
questions.discriminator_tested: GLBA = financial institutions.

questions.stem: What makes PCI DSS different from FERPA, FISMA, and GLBA?

options.text: It is an industry standard enforced through contracts with the card brands, not a government law
It is a US federal law
options.rationale: The other three are laws; PCI DSS is an industry standard.

options.text: It applies only to federal agencies

questions.explanation: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) protects cardholder data. It is an industry standard enforced through card-brand contracts, not a government law.
questions.discriminator_tested: PCI DSS is an industry standard, not a law.

questions.stem: After a breach, what separates reporting from notifications?

options.text: Reporting is the formal account to regulators, management, or auditors; notifications inform the affected individuals or customers within required timeframes
Reporting goes to customers; notifications go to auditors

options.rationale: They have different audiences and purposes.

options.text: Notifications go only to internal staff
options.rationale: Notifications go to the affected parties.

questions.explanation: Reporting is the formal reporting of incidents and compliance status to regulators, management, or auditors. Notifications inform affected individuals or customers within required timeframes.
questions.discriminator_tested: Reporting = authorities and oversight; notifications = affected parties.

questions.stem: After a breach exposes customers' personal data, the company must inform those customers before a legal deadline. What is this obligation?

options.text: Breach notifications, whose deadlines vary by law

options.rationale: The customers themselves have to be told.
That concerns where data is stored.

questions.explanation: Notifications inform affected individuals or customers (and sometimes regulators) after a breach, within required timeframes. The deadlines vary by law.
questions.discriminator_tested: Notifications go to affected parties; deadlines vary by law.
